extracted.intended_audience: regulators, policymakers, and policy analysts interested in data-driven regulatory reform (Canadian federal and provincial levels)
extracted.subtask_description: Using quantitative, text‑analysis derived indicators to identify and prioritize federal and provincial regulations that may need reform, by measuring restriction counts, applicability to industries, linguistic complexity, outdated language, and related features. The approach leverages NAICS mapping and machine learning on regulatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory restriction counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory restrictions are words and phrases in regulatory text that indicate specific obligations or prohibitions created by a regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RegData Canada datasets include counts of the following words and phrases: shall, may not, must, required, and prohibited. Use totals and distributions of these restriction-words in regulations to measure regulatory burden and to identify heavily prescriptive provisions for potential reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of regulations to economic sectors and industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the applicability of regulations to specific sectors and industries by mapping segments of regulatory text to industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use machine learning algorithms to map regulatory text to NAICS-based industries; this yields estimates of the number of restrictions and words that apply to specific sectors, enabling targeting of reform efforts to affected industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of incorporation by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how often regulations incorporate other documents or standards by reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevalence of incorporation by reference is reported as a quantitative indicator (listed among core dataset outputs). High prevalence may indicate reliance on external technical standards and potential complexity or hidden obligations; use counts/trends to prioritize review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic complexity — median sentence length
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare regulation complexity using median sentence length (median-length sentence in a document).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Median is used to avoid outliers (e.g., large tables). Canadian Treasury Board recommends 20 words per sentence; many regulations are at or below this, but those with median >20 words may require simplification or sentence-breaking to improve readability and reduce compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic complexity — Shannon entropy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Shannon entropy to measure the frequency of new ideas introduced in documents; simpler and more focused documents have lower entropy scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Average federal regulation entropy is 6.79. For comparison, Shakespeare's major plays are ~9.0–9.7. A suggested 'Shakespeare Test' flags regulations with entropy greater than Shakespeare's range for closer review to determine if they need simplification or updating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location of outdated language
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of regulatory text that use outdated or obsolete terminology or references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RegData reports the location of outdated language as an indicator; flagged language should be examined for potential updating or removal during reform exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood that a regulation includes prescriptive design standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate whether a regulation contains prescriptive design standards (detailed technical or design mandates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RegData includes indicators for the likelihood of prescriptive design standards. Regulations flagged as likely prescriptive may merit review to assess flexibility, innovation constraints, or unnecessary technical specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provincial and territorial restriction counts and cross-jurisdictional comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate restriction counts for each province and territory and compare across jurisdictions (and against sample US states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use province/territory datasets (13 datasets) to obtain total restriction counts as of July 2018. Cross-jurisdiction comparisons can reveal relative regulatory density and help prioritize provinces or sectors for reform; examples in the brief compare provinces and selected US states (e.g., New York, Idaho).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of restrictions by NAICS industries and provinces
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize restriction counts by substantive NAICS two-digit industries across provinces to show regulatory distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 5 style comparisons enable identification of which industries are more heavily regulated in which provinces (e.g., oil and gas extraction high in Alberta and Northwest Territories; finance and insurance abundant in British Columbia and Saskatchewan). Use such distributions to target industry-specific reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability and interactive tracking of datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide open access to the datasets and an interactive regulation tracker to enable stakeholders to explore and prioritize regulations for reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RegData Canada datasets and an interactive Canada Regulation Tracker are freely available at QuantGov.org; making data and tools public supports transparency, stakeholder engagement, and data-driven prioritization of reform opportunities.
